newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Protest death confusion in Kabila's Congo.
newsitem.headline: Protest death confusion in Kabila's Congo.

text.p: Up to three people died when soldiers opened fire on Friday to disperse opposition supporters in the capital of President Laurent Kabila's Congo, witnesses said. Officials said no one was killed in the incident.
Kabila's interior minister, Mwenze Kongolo, told state television that soldiers had fired in the air but denied that anyone had been killed.
The deaths, if confirmed, would be the first during an attempt by security forces to break up an opposition protest since Kabila toppled veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in May.

The marchers, from the radical PALU Unified Lumumbist Party loyal to the memory of slain nationalist independence leader Patrice Lumumba, were protesting against a ban by Kabila on political activity. Kabila says he too is a follower of Lumumba.
"The truth is that there were no deaths," Mwenze told state television, adding that four people had been wounded.
"The march was not authorised," he said. "It is clear there should be no political activity on Congolese territory. They knew that, they did what they did as an act of defiance."
Mwenze said the government would not tolerate laws being trampled on and said that the laws would be "strengthened to ensure order nationwide".
Kabila banned all political activity, including protest marches by opposition parties, shortly after taking power. He has also given himself wide-ranging powers as president.

"Soldiers in front of the foreign ministry opened fire while the crowd was coming back from the presidency where one Palu leader made a brief speech. It (the firing) was quite unexpected," said one witness unconnected with the march.

Earlier Mwenze's deputy, Faustin Munene, said that one person had been killed. "There was one person dead and two injured. The victim was hit by a stray bullet shot by other people than our soldiers," Munene told Reuters.
Earlier, state television, quoting witnesses, said several people died.
Kabila returned late on Friday from a trip to Eritrea.

Demonstrators marched through much of the city centre, from the main railway station to Kabila's offices. Witnesses said that at one point police beat them with truncheons and used teargas. Protesters chanted anti-government slogans.
Mwenze said they had tried to tear down a flag.

Witnesses said the march was peaceful and that soldiers around Kabila's offices in the city centre had initially fired into the air to disperse the crowd. The presidency is about one kilometre (mile) away from the foreign ministry.
Witnesses said five people were wounded.
One witness said one marcher had a pistol.
Most opposition protests to date have featured supporters or allies of veteran Mobutu opponent Etienne Tshisekedi, the main political opposition leader in the former Zaire.
Troops broke up early protests by firing in the air. They allowed some subsequent marches without intervening.
Soldiers briefly detained Tshisekedi for questioning on June 26 after he defied the ban to address students. They released him the next day.
Supporters of PALU, led by veteran opposition leader Antoine Gizenga, staged a protest in 1995 under Mobutu during which at least 10 people were killed.
